title: Basic Concepts of Polarization in Optics
short_intro: Polarization is a fundamental property of transverse waves, specifically electromagnetic waves, characterized by the restriction of the oscillation of the electric field vector to a single plane. It provides definitive proof of the transverse nature of light waves, as longitudinal waves cannot be polarized.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of polarized and unpolarized light, qualitative understanding of transverse waves, Malus's Law, polarization by reflection (Brewster's Law), and polaroids.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Mathematical description of linear, circular, and elliptic polarization, Jones vectors, analysis of states of polarization using quarter-wave and half-wave plates, and double refraction in uniaxial crystals.

prerequisites: Vector components and sinusoidal wave equations

concept_notes.heading: Nature of Unpolarized and Polarized Light
bullets: Unpolarized light (natural light) consists of rapid and random changes in the direction of the electric field vector E in the plane transverse to the direction of propagation.
Linearly polarized (or plane-polarized) light confines the vibration of the electric field vector E to a single fixed direction perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.
The intensity of unpolarized light can be represented as the sum of two mutually orthogonal, incoherent plane-polarized components of equal average intensity.

concept_notes.heading: Polarization by Reflection and Brewster's Law
bullets: When unpolarized light is incident on a transparent dielectric boundary at a specific angle called the polarizing angle or Brewster's angle (p), the reflected light is completely plane-polarized.
At Brewster's angle, the reflected ray and the refracted (transmitted) ray are mutually perpendicular to each other.
Brewster's law states that the tangent of the polarizing angle is equal to the relative refractive index of the denser medium with respect to the rarer medium.

concept_notes.heading: Malus's Law
bullets: Malus's law governs the intensity of plane-polarized light transmitted through an analyzer.

When completely plane-polarized light of intensity I_0 is incident on an analyzer whose transmission axis makes an angle θ with the plane of polarization of the incident light, the transmitted intensity is given by I = I_0 \cos^2 θ.
If unpolarized light is incident on an ideal polarizer, the transmitted intensity is exactly half of the initial unpolarized intensity, regardless of the orientation of the transmission axis.

concept_notes.heading: Double Refraction (Birefringence) and Optical Anisotropy
bullets: Certain crystals, such as calcite and quartz, split an unpolarized incident light ray into two refracted rays: the Ordinary ray (O-ray) and the Extraordinary ray (E-ray).
The O-ray obeys Snell's law of refraction and travels with the same velocity in all directions, whereas the E-ray does not obey Snell's law and its velocity varies with direction.
Uniaxial crystals possess a single optic axis along which the velocities of the O-ray and E-ray are identical.

derivations.title: Brewster's Law Derivation
derivations.conditions: Unpolarized light incident on a dielectric boundary at polarizing angle p
steps: Let light be incident at angle i_p such that the reflected ray is completely polarized.
According to Brewster's law, at angle of incidence i_p = i_p, the reflected ray and refracted ray (angle r) are perpendicular: i_p + r = 90\degree, hence r = 90\degree - i_p.
Applying Snell's Law at the interface: \frac{\sin i_p}{\sin r} = \mu_2 / \mu_1 = \mu.
Substitute r = 90\degree - i_p into Snell's law: \frac{\sin i_p}{\sin(90\degree - i_p)} = \frac{\sin i_p}{\cos i_p} = \tan i_p = \mu.

derivations.title: Intensity of Transmitted Light via Malus's Law
derivations.conditions: Plane-polarized electric field vector E_0 incident on an analyzer at angle θ
steps: Let the electric field vector of the incident polarized light be E_0 with amplitude \vec{E}_0.
When incident on an analyzer with a transmission axis at angle θ to E_0, resolve E_0 into two rectangular components: E_0 \cos θ parallel to the axis and E_0 \sin θ perpendicular to the axis.
The component that passes through the analyzer is the parallel component: E = E_0 \cos θ.
Since light intensity is proportional to the square of the electric field amplitude (I \propto E^2), the transmitted intensity I = I_0 \cos^2 θ.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Malus's Law Intensity Variation Plot
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A polar or Cartesian plot of transmitted intensity I versus angle θ showing symmetric lobes with maxima at 0\degree, 180\degree, 360\degree and zero intensity at 90\degree, 270\degree.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the cosine-squared dependence of light intensity passing through crossed and parallel polarizers.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual questions regarding rotating analyzers and identifying extinction points.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Polarization by Reflection Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Ray diagram showing unpolarized light striking a glass slab at angle i_p, with a reflected ray perpendicular to the refracted ray, indicating complete polarization of the reflected beam.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes Brewster's condition where the reflected beam contains only s-polarized light (electric field perpendicular to the plane of incidence).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in numerical problems to calculate refractive index given the angle of incidence.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Double Refraction in Calcite Crystal
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Unsplit ray entering a calcite crystal surface and splitting into ordinary (O) and extraordinary (E) rays bending at different angles.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates optical anisotropy and the existence of two distinct refractive indices in birefringent media.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core concept for PGT-level questions regarding wavefront propagation in crystals.

solved_numericals.question: At what angle of incidence should a ray of light be incident on the surface of water (refractive index = 1.33) so that the reflected light is completely polarized?

Unpolarized light of intensity 32 W/m^2 is passed through a polarizer. The transmitted light is then passed through an analyzer whose transmission axis makes an angle of 60\degree with the polarizer axis. Find the final transmitted intensity.
solution_steps: Find the intensity after the first polarizer: I_1 = \frac{1}{2} I_0 = \frac{1}{2} \times 32 = 16 \text{ W/m}^2.
Apply Malus's law for the analyzer with \theta = 60\degree: I = I_1 \cos^2(60\degree).

solved_numericals.question: A quarter-wave plate is designed for sodium light of wavelength \lambda = 589 \text{ nm}. If the principal refractive indices are n_e = 1.553 and n_o = 1.544, calculate the minimum thickness of the plate.
solution_steps: Identify the given parameters: \lambda = 589 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}, n_e = 1.553, n_o = 1.544.
Use the formula for the minimum thickness of a quarter-wave plate: t = \frac{\lambda}{4|n_e - n_o|}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Light is treated as a classical transverse electromagnetic wave, ignoring quantum photon polarization states in basic geometrical and wave optics contexts.
Polarizers and analyzers are assumed to be ideal (complete extinction at 90\degree and 100% transmission for parallel alignment), ignoring minor absorption and reflection losses at surfaces.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Longitudinal waves like sound waves can be polarized if given high enough amplitude.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only transverse waves can be polarized.
common_misconceptions.why: Polarization requires oscillations to occur in a plane perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation, which is impossible for longitudinal waves where oscillations are parallel to propagation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The sum of intensities when unpolarized light passes through two crossed polarizers is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: The transmitted intensity is 25% of the original unpolarized light intensity.
common_misconceptions.why: Unpolarized light becomes half-intensity polarized after the first polarizer (I_0/2), and applying Malus's law at 90\degree gives (I_0/2) \cos^2(90\degree) = 0? Wait, if there are three polarizers with the middle one at 45 degrees, intensity is non-zero. For two polarizers at 90 degrees, intensity is zero.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Brewster's law only applies to reflection from metallic surfaces.
common_misconceptions.correct: Brewster's law applies strictly to transparent dielectric media.
common_misconceptions.why: Metals possess complex refractive indices and high absorption coefficients, causing phase changes upon reflection that prevent complete linear polarization at a single angle.

quick_revision: Polarization confirms the transverse wave nature of light.
At Brewster's angle, reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular, and \mu = \tan i_p.
Malus's Law states that transmitted intensity varies as I = I_0 \cos^2 \theta.
Unpolarized light passing through an ideal polarizer drops to half its original intensity.
Birefringent crystals split unpolarized light into ordinary (O) and extraordinary (E) rays.
